summary: BBN's host status report for October 12 to 22, 1971, with a table of daily test results. It notes that the general state of hosts stayed the same. It was replaced by RFC 266.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 255 records the results of checks on ARPANET hosts from October 12 to October 22, 1971. It says their general status had not changed from the previous report, and RFC 266 later replaced it.

what did the arpanet host status codes mean
which hosts were reachable in october 1971
subtitle: A snapshot of ARPANET host accessibility from October 12 to 22, 1971

tldr.problem: Network operators needed a record of which listed hosts could be reached during the reporting period.
tldr.mechanism: The report records daily connection-test outcomes for hosts, using short codes for open, dead, timed out, half open and refused.
tldr.outcome: The report says the general status remained as before and was later replaced by RFC 266.

sections.title: The Reporting Period
sections.content:
RFC 255 reports the status of most Network Hosts from October 12 to October 22. It notes that October 11 was Columbus Day and was not included in this period.

The report's opening says the general status of the hosts remained as it had been previously. The tables provide the daily observations behind that statement.
sections.plainLanguage: This report covers host checks from October 12 through October 22. Its opening says the overall picture was unchanged from the earlier report.

sections.title: How to Read the Results
sections.content:
The tables list a network address, site, computer, date and test result for each observation. O means the host opened a connection and was accessible to a user. D means it was dead or inaccessible from the BBN Terminal IMP; T means no response to the initial RFC, although the host was not dead.

R means the host refused the initial request. H means it opened a connection and then immediately closed it or stopped responding. A footnote explains that a marked UCLA system offered Remote Job Service but not a full Telnet server, and another mark indicates a site might be unavailable at the test time.
sections.plainLanguage: The letters show what happened when a host was tested. Open means it was accessible; the other codes distinguish no response, refusal, partial connection, or inaccessibility.

sections.title: A Historical Status Snapshot
sections.content:
The report is a dated record, not a general guarantee that a host was always available. Each table entry reflects one test at the date and Eastern time shown.

The unit metadata records RFC 266 as the document that obsoleted RFC 255. The report itself focuses on the observations in its tables.
sections.plainLanguage: Each result describes one check at one listed time, not the host's availability at all times. RFC 266 later replaced this report.
